issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s ownership acquired under a statutory land-purchase scheme cannot be defeated by the landlord’s death during an appeal when the tenant had qualified to purchase and deposited the first instalment before that death.
material_facts: The landlord was a large landowner when the tenants applied to purchase the land, and the tenants were found eligible.
The purchase price and instalments were fixed, and each tenant deposited the first instalment.
Under the statutory scheme, depositing the first instalment caused ownership to vest in the tenant.
The landlord died while the appeals were pending, and the heirs’ shares made them small landowners.
The heirs argued that the appeal was a continuation of the original proceeding and that their later status as small landowners deprived the tenants of the right to purchase.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ ownership had vested upon deposit of the first instalment and was not undone by the landlord’s subsequent death or the heirs’ resulting status as small landowners. The appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 18(1) and 18(4) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953, a qualifying tenant of a landlord who is not a small landowner is entitled to purchase the land, and deposit of the first instalment makes the tenant its owner. Section 2(2) defines the small-landowner category. Rights are generally determined by the facts existing when the proceeding is instituted; later events may exceptionally affect the form of relief, including where the relief becomes obsolete, is discretionary, or the governing statute makes later facts relevant. But later events cannot divest a statutory right that has already vested, except where a change in law is made applicable at any stage. The Court relied on P. Venkateswarlu v. Motor & General Traders, Bhajan Lal v. State of Punjab, Patterson v. State of Alabama, Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri, and Ramji Lal v. State of Punjab, and applied the principle that an act of the court shall prejudice no one.

rule.if: tenant_purchase_proceeding and tenant_eligible_when_applied and landlord_large_at_application and tenant_deposited_first_installment and first_installment_triggers_ownership and landlord_died_during_appeal and heirs_became_small_landowners

predicates.tenant_purchase_proceeding: A tenant sought to purchase land from a landlord under a statutory land-purchase scheme.
predicates.tenant_eligible_when_applied: The tenant met the scheme’s eligibility requirements when applying to purchase the land.
predicates.landlord_large_at_application: The landlord was not within the scheme’s small-landowner category when the tenant applied.
predicates.tenant_deposited_first_installment: The tenant deposited the first instalment of the purchase price.
predicates.first_installment_triggers_ownership: The applicable purchase scheme provided that depositing the first instalment vested ownership in the tenant.
predicates.landlord_died_during_appeal: The landlord died while an appeal concerning the purchase was pending.
predicates.heirs_became_small_landowners: Succession divided the landlord’s holding so that the heirs fell within the small-landowner category.
predicates.vested_tenant_ownership_survives_later_l: The tenant’s ownership, once vested, is not defeated by the landlord’s later death or a resulting change in the heirs’ landowner status.

issues.definition: When an eligible tenant purchases land from a landlord outside the small-landowner category and deposits the instalment that vests ownership, the ownership survives the landlord’s later death and any resulting change in the heirs’ status.

issues.legal_issue: A valuation challenge dependent on the classification of land cannot be considered for the first time on appeal when its factual foundation was neither put in issue nor considered below.
material_facts: The appeals concerned compensation payable to landholders for land that had vested in tenants.
The appellants sought to contest whether the land was irrigated or non-irrigated for valuation purposes and raised the meaning of similar land in the valuation scheme.
The land’s nature had not been put in issue or considered in the High Court, and deciding the challenge would require an inquiry into facts not raised at the prior level.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the newly raised valuation issue because it required factual inquiry without a factual foundation below. The appeals were dismissed without costs.
issues.legal_principle: A court will not decide on appeal a new issue requiring factual inquiry when the relevant factual foundation was not raised or considered in the court below. The Court therefore did not decide the substantive meaning of similar land under section 18(2) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953.

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for land transferred under a statutory purchase scheme.
predicates.land_classification_not_put_in_issue_bel: The appellant did not place the land’s relevant classification in issue before the lower court.
predicates.land_classification_not_considered_below: The lower court did not consider the land’s relevant classification.
predicates.valuation_challenge_requires_new_factual: Resolving the appellant’s valuation challenge would require a factual inquiry not undertaken below.
predicates.new_factual_valuation_challenge_not_ente: The appellate court does not entertain a valuation challenge that depends on facts not raised and considered below.

issues.definition: In a compensation appeal, a valuation challenge requiring factual inquiry is not entertained when the relevant land classification was neither raised nor considered below.
